rounds.hypothesis: The set_mode() implementation is a no-op that returns Ok(()) without changing any state, causing chmod to succeed but stat to show unchanged permissions
rounds.change: Added in-memory cached_mode field to ExfatInodeInner to store chmod-set permissions. Modified make_mode() to return cached mode if set, otherwise compute from FAT attributes. Modified set_mode() to store the mode in cached_mode.
rounds.outcome: Test passed: all 32 checks passed (16 chmod + 16 stat for files and directories)

layer: Filesystem implementation layer (ExfatInode). The ownership is correct - this is where permission semantics are implemented per filesystem. While the diagnose phase suggested returning EPERM to match Linux, Asterinas takes a different approach by caching permissions in memory to provide chmod functionality even though the on-disk format doesn't support it.
generalizes: This fix applies to all chmod operations on exfat filesystems in Asterinas. Any code calling chmod/fchmod/fchmodat on exfat files will now see correct semantics - permissions are cached and reflected in subsequent stat calls. The permissions are stored in-memory only and don't persist across unmount/remount, which is a reasonable tradeoff since exfat has no on-disk representation for UNIX permissions. No other filesystem is affected since this change is isolated to the ExfatInode implementation.
fix_summary: The fix implements in-memory permission caching for exfat inodes. Added a cached_mode: Option<InodeMode> field that stores chmod-set permissions for the lifetime of the mount. This is an Asterinas-specific extension - Linux's exfat driver returns EPERM for chmod, but Asterinas provides working chmod semantics by maintaining the mode in memory. The abstraction follows Asterinas's Inode trait design where each filesystem implements set_mode/mode according to its capabilities. This approach balances compatibility (chmod works as expected) with filesystem semantics (exfat doesn't persist permissions to disk).
